facts.name: Addition Principle for Mutually Exclusive Cases
facts.content: When a selection can occur in several mutually exclusive cases, the total number of selections is the sum of the counts from each case.

facts.name: Conditions for a Binomial Model
facts.content: A random variable follows a binomial distribution B(n, p) if there is a fixed number of trials n, each trial has only two mutually exclusive outcomes (success/failure), the probability of success p is constant across all trials, and the trials are independent.

facts.name: Class Midpoint Calculation
facts.content: The midpoint of a class interval with lower boundary a and upper boundary b is \dfrac{a + b}{2}.

facts.name: Class Midpoint for Grouped Mean
facts.content: The estimated mean of grouped continuous data uses class midpoints x = (lower limit + upper limit) / 2 to weight frequencies.

facts.name: Combined Mean of Two Groups
facts.content: \bar{x} = \frac{n_1 \bar{x}_1 + n_2 \bar{x}_2}{n_1 + n_2}

facts.name: Complement Rule of Probability
facts.content: \mathrm{P}(A') = 1 - \mathrm{P}(A)

facts.name: Continuity Correction for Greater Than or Equal To
facts.content: \mathrm{P}(Y \ge r) \approx \mathrm{P}\left(X_{\text{cont}} > r - 0.5\right)

facts.name: Continuity Correction for Strict Lower Bound on Discrete Variables
facts.statement: When approximating a discrete random variable X taking integer values by a continuous distribution Y, the strict inequality P(X > k) = P(X >= k + 1) is represented on the continuous scale by P(Y > k + 0.5).

facts.name: Continuity Correction for Strict Upper Bound on Discrete Variables
facts.statement: When approximating a discrete random variable X taking integer values by a continuous distribution W, the event P(X < k) = P(X <= k - 1) is represented on the continuous scale by P(W < k - 0.5).

facts.name: Class Frequency from Cumulative Frequency
facts.content: The frequency of a class interval (a, b] is given by \mathrm{CF}(b) - \mathrm{CF}(a).

facts.name: Plotting Cumulative Frequencies at Upper Class Boundaries
facts.content: In a cumulative frequency graph for continuous grouped data, cumulative frequencies are plotted at the upper boundary of each class interval, starting at (lower boundary of first class, 0).

facts.name: Five-Number Summary for Box Plots
facts.content: A box plot displays the minimum value, lower quartile (Q1), median (Q2), upper quartile (Q3), and maximum value.

facts.name: Grouped Frequency Table Invariance Under Within-Class Data Shifts
facts.statement: When individual values in a grouped frequency dataset are altered or corrected in such a way that each altered value remains within its original class boundaries, all class frequencies and class midpoints remain unchanged, and consequently the calculated estimates of the mean and standard deviation remain identical.

facts.name: Histogram Area Proportionality
facts.content: In a histogram, the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency of the corresponding class interval.

facts.name: Histogram Area Proportionality
facts.content: In a histogram, the area of each bar is proportional to frequency, and height equals frequency density = frequency / class width.

facts.name: Definition of Independent Events
facts.content: Two events A and B are independent if and only if P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B) or P(A|B) = P(A).

facts.name: Law of Total Probability
facts.content: For a partition {A, H}, the total probability of event C is \mathrm{P}(C) = \mathrm{P}(A \cap C) + \mathrm{P}(H \cap C) = \mathrm{P}(A)\mathrm{P}(C \mid A) + \mathrm{P}(H)\mathrm{P}(C \mid H).

facts.name: Effect of Linear Coding on Mean
facts.content: If y = a*x + b, then the mean of y is given by y_bar = a * x_bar + b.

facts.name: Invariance of Standard Deviation Under Constant Shift
facts.content: Adding or subtracting a constant shift a to each data value translates the distribution without altering its dispersion, so \operatorname{sd}(x - a) = \operatorname{sd}(x).

facts.name: Sum of Linearly Shifted Data
facts.content: \sum (x - a) = \sum x - n a for any constant shift a over n data values.

facts.name: Effect of Linear Coding on Variance
facts.content: If y = a*x + b, then Var(y) = a^2 * Var(x) and sigma_y = |a| * sigma_x; adding a constant does not affect dispersion.

facts.name: Invariance of Variance Under Linear Shift
facts.content: \operatorname{Var}(x - a) = \operatorname{Var}(x)

facts.name: Logarithmic Inequality Sign Reversal
facts.content: When solving a^n < b where 0 < a < 1, taking logarithms yields n \ln(a) < \ln(b). Because \ln(a) < 0, dividing by \ln(a) reverses the inequality to n > \ln(b) / \ln(a).

facts.name: Sensitivity of Mean to Outliers
facts.statement: The arithmetic mean uses every value in a dataset and is therefore disproportionately affected by extreme values or outliers, whereas the median is resistant to extreme values.

facts.name: Definition of Mode
facts.content: \text{The mode is the value that occurs with the highest frequency in a data set.}

facts.name: Fundamental Principle of Counting
facts.content: If a sequence of k choices has n_1, n_2, ..., n_k options respectively, the total number of sequential outcomes is n_1 \times n_2 \times ... \times n_k.

facts.name: Conditions for Normal Approximation to Binomial
facts.content: A normal approximation to a binomial distribution B(n, p) is valid when both np > 5 and n(1 - p) > 5.

facts.name: Standard Normal Cumulative Probability Function
facts.content: \mathrm{P}(Z < z) = \Phi(z) for standard normal variable Z.

facts.name: Symmetry and Bell Shape of the Normal Distribution
facts.content: A normal distribution is unimodal, bell-shaped, and symmetric about its mean, with frequencies tapering smoothly towards zero in both tails.

facts.name: Symmetry of Standard Normal Lower Tail
facts.content: For a standard normal distribution, \Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z). A tail probability in the lower 5% corresponds to z = -\Phi^{-1}(0.95) = -1.645.

facts.name: Normal Upper Tail at Negative Z
facts.content: \mathrm{P}(Z > -z) = \mathrm{P}(Z < z) = \Phi(z) by symmetry of the normal distribution curve about 0.

facts.name: Upper-Tail Probability of a Normal Distribution
facts.content: \mathrm{P}(Z > z) = 1 - \Phi(z) \text{ for } z > 0

facts.name: Condition for an Integer to be Odd
facts.content: An integer is odd if and only if its units digit is from the set \{1, 3, 5, 7, 9\}.

facts.name: 1.5 x IQR Outlier Rule
facts.content: \text{Outliers lie strictly below } Q_1 - 1.5 \times IQR \text{ or strictly above } Q_3 + 1.5 \times IQR

facts.name: Selection with Predetermined Items
facts.content: If k specific items must be included in a selection of size r from n items, the number of choices is \binom{n - k}{r - k}.

facts.name: Quartile Positions on Cumulative Frequency Graph
facts.content: For total frequency N, the lower quartile Q_1, median Q_2, and upper quartile Q_3 correspond to cumulative frequencies 0.25N, 0.5N, and 0.75N.

facts.name: Number of Observations Exceeding a Value from Cumulative Frequency
facts.content: The number of observations greater than a threshold x is given by N - \mathrm{cf}(x), where N is total frequency and \mathrm{cf}(x) is the cumulative frequency at x.

facts.name: Selection Without Replacement
facts.content: When items are selected without replacement from a finite pool, the total number of items and category counts decrease by 1 after each draw.

facts.name: Discrepancy Between Mean and Median Indicates Skewness
facts.statement: In a distribution that is not symmetrical (skewed), the mean and median will differ; if the mean is less than the median, the distribution is typically negatively skewed, while if the mean is greater than the median, it is positively skewed.

facts.name: Total Sum from Sample Mean
facts.content: For n observations with mean \bar{x}, the total sum is \sum x = n \bar{x}.

facts.name: Sum of Probabilities in a Discrete Distribution
facts.content: For any discrete random variable X, \sum \mathrm{P}(X = x) = 1 over all possible values.

facts.name: Sum of Probabilities in a Discrete Distribution
facts.content: \sum \mathrm{P}(X = x) = 1

facts.name: Condition for Independence of Two Events
facts.content: Events A and B are independent if and only if \mathrm{P}(A \cap B) = \mathrm{P}(A)\mathrm{P}(B); if \mathrm{P}(A \cap B) \ne \mathrm{P}(A)\mathrm{P}(B), they are not independent.

facts.name: Zero Standard Deviation Implies Identical Data Values
facts.content: A standard deviation of zero implies that there is no dispersion in the dataset, meaning every observation is identical and equal to the mean.
